item.title: Product Strategy ≠ Template
item.description:
The goal of strategy is to move from «we build whatever anyone asks for» to a considered position aimed at creating a better future for both users and the business.

As much as we’d like one to exist, there is no universal product strategy template — no template at all, really. The format depends on the company’s maturity, the team’s experience, organizational structure, business model, business strategy, and a huge number of other factors.

item.title: Prioritization Methods: ICE, RICE, DRICE
item.description: Eins, zwei, drei… There are endless ways to prioritize tasks. Every product I’ve ever worked on had its own original approach to ranking projects — each with its own quirks. For a quick tour of the methods used at major companies, check out Misha Karpov’s talk at a Yandex product meetup [1]. As for my personal favorites — there’s the energy-based method, where priorities shift depending on how you’re feeling, and the intuitive method, where you just listen to your gut. The only problem is that teams rarely agree to go along with either approach.

item.title: The Evolution of Goal-Setting Frameworks: From OKR to NCT
item.description:
I came across an interesting approach to goal-setting — NCT (Narratives, Commitments, Tasks) by Ravi Mehta [1]. What makes it compelling is that it positions itself as an alternative to OKR and could be genuinely useful for many product teams. Before diving into NCT, let’s take a quick look at the history of goal-setting frameworks.

In 1954, Peter Drucker introduced the concept of MBO (Management by Objectives) in his book The Practice of Management [2]. The core idea: set goals at the company level and cascade them down to individual contributors at every level. Many services within Yandex, for instance, still use a similar approach today. They even have a dedicated internal tool for cascading goals called «Golzyatnitsa» (roughly, «the goal keeper»).

item.title: The Growth Dilemma of Educational Course Economics
item.description:
Looking at the top edTech companies in the Russian-speaking internet market, I noticed an interesting scaling problem baked into the economics of their courses — one they’ve simply learned to live with. I’m not talking about product-led edTech platforms like Lingualeo, but companies that create educational courses for upskilling or career transitions.

Product EdTech Theorem #1

The absence of deadlines in an educational course leads to ↑ Revenue and ↓ Completion Rate (COR). Conversely, having deadlines leads to ↓ Revenue and ↑ Completion Rate.

item.title: ICE, RICE, DRICE Prioritization Template
item.description:
A Google Sheets template for prioritizing product initiatives using three methods: ICE, RICE, and DRICE. For a deeper dive into the methods, see the article «ICE, RICE, DRICE Prioritization Methods».

Download the template

What’s inside

ICE is the simplest prioritization method. Each initiative is scored on three parameters from 0 to 10:

  • Impact (effect on the metric)
  • Confidence (confidence in the estimate)
  • Ease (ease of implementation)
  • ICE Score = I × C × E
